results.title: $p$-neighbors of submodules
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $M$ an $R$-module and $p$ a natural number. Two submodules $L_1$ and $L_2$ of $M$ are $p$-neighbors when $p$ is prime and the intersection $L_1 \cap L_2$ has index $p$ in each of them, that is, the quotients $L_1 / (L_1 \cap L_2)$ and $L_2 / (L_1 \cap L_2)$ both have exactly $p$ elements.

results.title: The $p$-neighbor relation is symmetric
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $p$ and all submodules $L_1$, $L_2$ of a module $M$ over a commutative ring $R$, $L_1$ and $L_2$ are $p$-neighbors if and only if $L_2$ and $L_1$ are $p$-neighbors.

results.title: No submodules are $1$-neighbors
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For any submodules $L_1$ and $L_2$ of a module $M$ over a commutative ring $R$, $L_1$ and $L_2$ are not $1$-neighbors, since $1$ is not prime.

results.summary: For an integer $k$, the quadratic Gauss sum $g(k; 5)$ is the complex number $g(k; 5) = \sum_{n=0}^{4} e^{2\pi i k n^2 / 5}$.

results.title: Russo–Dye theorem

results.title: Stinespring dilation theorem

results.title: Number of weak ascents of a word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a word $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_m$ of natural numbers, $\mathrm{wasc}(a_1 \cdots a_m)$ is the number of weak ascents, that is, of positions $j$ with $1 \le j < m$ and $a_j \le a_{j+1}$; in particular the empty word and every word of length one have no weak ascents.

results.title: Weak ascent sequence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A word $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ over $\mathbb{N}$ is a weak ascent sequence if either $n = 0$, or $a_1 = 0$ and $a_i \le 1 + \operatorname{wasc}(a_1 \cdots a_{i-1})$ for every $2 \le i \le n$, where $\operatorname{wasc}(u)$ is the number of weak ascents of $u$, that is, of positions $j$ with $u_j \le u_{j+1}$.

results.title: Pattern containment in words
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A word $w$ over $\mathbb{N}$ contains a pattern $p$ (another word over $\mathbb{N}$) if $w$ has a subsequence $s$, not necessarily contiguous, of the same length as $p$ that is order-isomorphic to $p$: for all positions $i$ and $j$, $s_i < s_j$ if and only if $p_i < p_j$.

results.title: The thirteen patterns of length three
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Ascent sequences avoiding a set of patterns
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite set $P$ of patterns (words over $\mathbb{N}$) and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $A_n(P)$ is the set of ascent sequences of length $n$ that contain no pattern of $P$.

results.title: Weak ascent sequences avoiding a set of patterns
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite set $P$ of patterns (words over $\mathbb{N}$) and a natural number $n$, $\mathrm{WA}_n(P)$ is the set of weak ascent sequences of length $n$ that contain none of the patterns in $P$.

results.title: Position of the last descent top
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite sequence $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_m$ of natural numbers, a descent of $w$ is an index $1 \le i < m$ with $w_i > w_{i+1}$, and $w_i$ is its descent top. The position of the last descent top of $w$ is the largest index $i$ with $w_i > w_{i+1}$ (positions counted from $1$), and it is $0$ if $w$ has no descent.

results.title: Saturating non-edge
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F$ and $G$ be simple graphs. A pair of vertices $x, y$ of $G$ is an $F$-saturating non-edge of $G$ if $x \ne y$, $x$ and $y$ are not adjacent in $G$, and the graph $G + xy$ obtained from $G$ by adding the edge $xy$ contains a copy of $F$ (a subgraph isomorphic to $F$, not necessarily induced).

results.title: A saturating non-edge of an $F$-free graph creates a copy of $F$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ and $G$ be simple graphs, and let $xy$ be an $F$-saturating non-edge of $G$. If $G$ is $F$-free, that is, $G$ contains no copy of $F$, then the graph $G + xy$ obtained from $G$ by adding the edge $xy$ contains a copy of $F$, and $G$ does not.

results.title: Graph of saturating non-edges
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F$ and $G$ be simple graphs. The graph of $F$-saturating non-edges of $G$ is the simple graph on the vertices of $G$ whose edges are exactly the $F$-saturating non-edges of $G$.

results.title: Number of saturating non-edges
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $F$ and $G$ be simple graphs such that $G$ has only finitely many $F$-saturating non-edges. Then $f_F(G)$ is the number of $F$-saturating non-edges of $G$, counted as unordered pairs $\{x, y\}$, that is, the number of edges of the graph of $F$-saturating non-edges of $G$.

results.title: $H$-saturated graphs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph. A simple graph $G$ is $H$-saturated if $G$ is $H$-free (it contains no copy of $H$ as a subgraph) and is maximal with this property: every $H$-free simple graph $G'$ on the same vertex set as $G$ with $G \subseteq G'$ equals $G$.

results.title: Saturation via strict supergraphs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph. A simple graph $G$ is $H$-saturated if and only if $G$ is $H$-free and every simple graph $G'$ on the same vertex set with $G \subsetneq G'$ contains a copy of $H$.

results.title: Saturation via missing edges
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph. A simple graph $G$ is $H$-saturated if and only if $G$ is $H$-free and, for all distinct vertices $s$ and $t$ of $G$ that are not adjacent in $G$, the graph $G + st$ obtained from $G$ by adding the edge $st$ contains a copy of $H$.

results.title: Saturation of complete graphs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph. The complete graph on any vertex set is $H$-saturated if and only if it is $H$-free.

results.title: Edge counts of saturated graphs
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph and $n$ a natural number. The set of saturated edge counts of $H$ on $n$ vertices is the set of natural numbers $m$ such that some $H$-saturated simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ has exactly $m$ edges.

results.title: Saturation number
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph and $n$ a natural number. The saturation number $\operatorname{sat}(n, H)$ is the minimum number of edges of an $H$-saturated simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$, and is $0$ when no such graph exists.

results.title: The saturation number is zero when no saturated graph exists
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph, $n$ a natural number, and $\operatorname{sat}(n, H)$ the saturation number of $H$ on $n$ vertices. If the set of saturated edge counts of $H$ on $n$ vertices is empty, that is, no $H$-saturated simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ exists, then $\operatorname{sat}(n, H) = 0$.

results.title: Saturated graphs bound the saturation number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $H$ be a simple graph, $n$ a natural number, and $\operatorname{sat}(n, H)$ the saturation number of $H$ on $n$ vertices. Every $H$-saturated simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, 1, \dots, n - 1\}$ has at least $\operatorname{sat}(n, H)$ edges.

results.title: Saturation number is attained by a saturated graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Attainment: when a saturated graph exists, some saturated graph has exactly `sat(n, H)` edges.

results.title: Strip packing instances

results.summary: A strip packing instance is a triple $(R, W, H)$ consisting of a finite list $R = ((w_1, h_1), \dots, (w_n, h_n))$ of pairs of natural numbers, the widths and heights of the rectangles, a natural number $W$, the width of the strip, and a natural number $H$, the height bound.

results.title: Well-formed strip packing instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A strip packing instance $(R, W, H)$ is well formed when every rectangle $(w, h)$ in the list $R$ has $w > 0$ and $h > 0$.

results.title: Feasible strip packings
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A strip packing instance $(R, W, H)$ with $R = ((w_1, h_1), \dots, (w_n, h_n))$ is feasible when there are natural numbers $x_1, y_1, \dots, x_n, y_n$ such that $x_j + w_j \le W$ and $y_j + h_j \le H$ for every $1 \le j \le n$, and for all $1 \le a < b \le n$ at least one of $x_a + w_a \le x_b$, $x_b + w_b \le x_a$, $y_a + h_a \le y_b$ and $y_b + h_b \le y_a$ holds.

results.title: The STRIP PACKING decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: STRIP PACKING is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of strip packing instances, to a strip packing instance that is well formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do not decode to a strip packing instance are rejected.

results.title: STRIP PACKING is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The STRIP PACKING decision problem belongs to NP, and every decision problem $L$ in NP reduces to STRIP PACKING by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

part.title: Saturation power for cancer gene discovery

path: Saturation power for cancer gene discovery

results.title: Saturation power of the binomial gene discovery test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Power of the one-sided binomial test of Lawrence et al. (2014): the probability, when each of `N` patients is mutated with probability `p₁`, of observing a count `x` whose background p-value `ℙ_{p₀}(X ≥ x)` is at most `γ`.

results.title: Background mutation probability per patient
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Background probability `p₀ = 1 - (1 - μ f_g)^(3L/4)` that a patient carries at least one non-silent background mutation in a gene of `L` coding bases (Lawrence et al. 2014).

results.title: Signal mutation probability per patient
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Signal probability `p₁ = p₀ + r (1 - m)` for a gene mutated in a fraction `r` of patients above background, with miss rate `m` (Lawrence et al. 2014).

results.title: Power tends to one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `0 ≤ p₀ < p₁ ≤ 1` and any level `γ > 0`, the power of the binomial test tends to `1` as the number of patients grows.

results.title: `N_β` exists
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every target power `β < 1` there is a cohort size beyond which the power is at least `β` (Lawrence et al. 2014 take `β = 0.9`).

results.title: Background mutation probability lies in (0, 1)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The background probability is a probability below one: `0 ≤ p₀ < 1` for `0 ≤ μ f_g < 1` and `L ≥ 0`.

results.title: Driver genes raise the per-patient mutation probability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A driver mutated above background raises the per-patient probability: `p₀ < p₀ + r (1 - m)` for `r > 0` and `m < 1`.
